title: Fix Joust graphical bug
description: Joust has a graphical rendering bug that needs investigation and fixing.
close_reason: Root cause: M6809 TST <memory> (0x0D/0x6D/0x7D) erroneously wrote the operand back through the RMW helper. On real hardware TST reads + does dummy VMA cycles, no store (confirmed vs MAME TST8 microcode). Under Williams ROM banking a read returns ROM but the write lands in VRAM, so the boot text-print loop (TST ,U+ over a ROM message table) smeared ROM bytes into video RAM — the frame-447 vertical strip. Fixed: TST's final RMW cycle now does a dummy VMA read instead of a write. Verified full VRAM byte-identical to MAME 0.287 at frame 447. Added regression tests.

title: Concrete bus dispatch: TKG-04 (Donkey Kong, DK Jr, Mario Bros)
description:
Convert the TKG-04 board (Z80 + I8035 sound + DMA) to concrete bus dispatch per docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md. Three machines on one board and no reset-vector CPU, so this is the highest-value unblocked step after the prototypes.

Move cpu/sound_cpu out of Tkg04Board into the game wrappers, decide per game whether the board can be the bus outright or needs a view, split once per frame, and check the DMA path's bus master handling. Measure dkong before/after with phosphor-bench; run golden frames.
close_reason:
Done in 1372bb6.

Correction to the issue premise: Mario Bros is NOT on the TKG-04 board. It has its own MarioBrosBoard with a Z80 DMA and shares only the palette/monitor model with tkg04.rs. Converted it alongside DK and DK Jr anyway since the issue named it.

Numbers (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, best of 6 alternating runs, idle host):
  dkong     1.161 -> 0.966 ms/f  -16.8%
  mariobros 1.238 -> 1.017       -17.8%
The largest gains of the rollout so far -- 3.072 MHz boards at 50,688 cycles/frame, so almost all of the frame is CPU cycles and bus accesses. (DK Jr not benchmarked: the reference ROM collection has no revision it can boot -- the same reason it carries an [[unpinned]] golden-frame entry.)

Shapes used, one of each:
- Mario Bros: the board IS the bus (impl Bus for MarioBrosBoard), CPUs on the machine, tick takes them directly -- no trait, no view, since only one machine uses that board.
- DK / DK Jr: a newtype view over the shared board (struct DkongBus<'a>(&'a mut Tkg04Board)), because their address decoding differs while the state behind it is all board. Single pointer, hoisted per frame -- none of the multi-pointer view cost the Galaga prototype found.

Neither board's DMA is a bus master in the trait sense: TKG-04's sprite DMA and Mario's Z80Dma both move bytes through the address space directly (main_map), not through Bus, so no lift was needed (unlike Williams' blitter).

New wrinkle worth recording for the remaining conversions: the sound CPU's *ports* are bus-visible. The I8035 reads its own P1/P2 back through io_read, and DK's main CPU reads P2 bit 4 as a sound-busy bit -- so with the CPU outside the bus, the board keeps a cycle-fresh mirror (sound_p1/sound_p2), latched in begin_cycle_inner before either CPU steps. Faithful because only the sound CPU writes those ports and it steps later in the same cycle. Derived state, not saved.

Also inverted both boards' frame loops to scanline-outer / cycle-inner, and renamed MarioBrosBoard::check_interrupts to interrupt_state so the Bus method of the same name can call it without recursing (the compiler caught this as 'function cannot return without recursing').

Golden frames unchanged for all pinned machines; machine, harness and ROM-gated suites pass; clippy and fmt clean.

title: Q*Bert speech too slow: Votrax clock hardcoded to 720 kHz, speech-clock DAC unimplemented
description:
Q*Bert's Votrax SC-01 speech plays back noticeably slower than on real hardware.

## Root cause

The Gottlieb Rev 1 sound/speech board drives the Votrax SC-01's master clock with
a writable VCO controlled by a "speech clock DAC" mapped at 0x3000 on the sound
CPU. The game writes this DAC to set (and dynamically vary) the speech rate/pitch.

In phosphor this is unimplemented in two places:

- machines/src/gottlieb.rs:290-291 — the DAC write is a no-op stub:
      // Speech clock DAC: 0x3000-0x3FFF (stub — adjusts Votrax VCO)
      0x3000..=0x3FFF => {}
- machines/src/gottlieb.rs:92 — the Votrax master clock is hardcoded:
      const VOTRAX_CLOCK_HZ: u64 = 720_000;
  with a fixed divider 18/125 (gottlieb.rs:94-95, used at :144, :434, :889).

Because the DAC is ignored, the Votrax always runs at a fixed 720 kHz instead of
the rate the game requests, and the speech rate never varies.

## What MAME does

src/mame/shared/gottlieb_a.cpp:
- :419  convert_speech_clock(data) = 950000 + (data - 0xa0) * 5500
- :426  speech_clock_dac_w() -> m_votrax->set_unscaled_clock(convert_speech_clock(data))
- :438  the 0x3000 (mirror 0x0fff) write maps to speech_clock_dac_w
- :471  device is created with convert_speech_clock(0) as the initial clock

So the nominal clock (data=0xa0) is 950 kHz and the game adjusts it from there.
phosphor's fixed 720 kHz is ~76% of the 950 kHz nominal, i.e. speech runs roughly
24% too slow — consistent with the reported symptom — and the game's intended
pitch/rate variation is lost entirely.

## Fix sketch

1. Implement the 0x3000-0x3FFF write: compute clock = 950000 + (data - 0xa0)*5500
   and push it to the Votrax (add a set_clock/set_unscaled_clock on VotraxSc01 in
   core/src/device/votrax_sc01.rs that recomputes sclock/cclock from the new clock).
2. Make the gottlieb sound-board <-> votrax clock divider track the current Votrax
   clock instead of the fixed VOTRAX_CLOCK_NUM/DEN (18/125), since the divider
   ratio against the 5 MHz timebase changes with the DAC value.
3. Initialize the Votrax clock from convert_speech_clock(0) to match MAME's
   construction default.

## Verification

After the fix, compare Q*Bert speech rate against MAME (gottlieb1_votrax /
GOTTLIEB_SOUND_SPEECH_REV1A) — durations should match and pitch should vary as
the game writes the DAC.
close_reason: Implemented the speech-clock DAC (sound CPU 0x3000): it now retunes the Votrax SC-01 VCO via convert_speech_clock (950 kHz nominal at 0xA0, ±5.5 kHz/step), matching MAME. The board re-derives the Votrax tick divider and the device's internal sclock/cclock + resampler rate whenever the DAC changes (and after state load). Default clock raised from the incorrect fixed 720 kHz to the 950 kHz nominal, fixing the too-slow speech.

title: Generalize display aspect-ratio handling (Renderable hint + frontend presentation)
description:
Aspect-ratio handling is currently ad-hoc per machine: Star Wars bakes a horizontal stretch into display_width + render (anamorphic); Burgertime bakes a vertical stretch into display_size (240x320) with a per-frame CPU nearest-neighbor upscale in render_frame. Most raster machines report their native raster and rely on it approximating the tube aspect, so any machine whose raster isn't its tube aspect (e.g. a 256x256 game on a 4:3 tube) is subtly wrong (square pixels).

Proposal: keep Renderable::display_size() as the true render resolution (native raster) and add a display-aspect hint (e.g. display_aspect_ratio() -> f32, default = native square, or an Option<(w,h)>). The frontend does aspect correction once at presentation time (size the window to the aspect, letterbox, let the GPU sample the texture). Machines like Burgertime/Star Wars set the hint instead of baking a lossy upscale into render_frame.

Benefits: correctness for every non-square-pixel machine; crisper output (one GPU stretch vs CPU nearest-neighbor + integer scale); native-resolution renders stay testable in native coords; removes per-machine bake duplication.

Scope/risks: touches core Renderable trait; frontend window-sizing / scale / egui side-panel layout (all keyed off display_size today, see frontend/src/emulator.rs and video.rs); needs a visual re-verification pass across machines to set correct aspects and catch regressions.

Migration: after the mechanism lands, migrate Burgertime (drop the 240x320 stretch in machines/src/btime.rs render_frame, set 3:4 hint) and Star Wars (drop the display_width=400 anamorphic bake) to the hint, and audit other raster machines for correct aspect.
close_reason: Generalized display aspect handling: display_aspect hint on TimingConfig/Renderable, presentation-time correction in the frontend (window sizing, unified letterbox, vector viewport), migrated Burgertime (3:4) and Star Wars (true 4:3) off their bakes, and set 4:3/3:4 hints across all raster + vector machines. Visually verified.

title: Concrete bus dispatch: Atari System 1 and Gottlieb System 80
description:
Convert Marble Madness and Road Runner (M68000, the bus_split! 'u32 word' arm and impl_board_delegation's bus_addr option) and Q*bert (I8088 + M6502, the 'u32' arm), per docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md. Blocked by the generic Cpu::reset task.

Nothing about the conversion is width-specific: the bus_split! arms exist only to name the trait object's type parameters and disappear with it. Marble is the slowest board in the bench set, so measure it carefully.
close_reason:
Done in 926a5af (marble + roadrunner on Atari System 1; qbert on Gottlieb System 80).

Numbers (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, best of 6 alternating runs, idle host):
  roadrunner 1.634 -> 1.387 ms/f  -15.1%
  marble     2.169 -> 1.902       -12.3%
  qbert      2.797 -> 2.777        -0.7%

Q*bert is the one board in the whole rollout that gained essentially nothing, and the cause is specific: its ~2.8 ms/frame is dominated by the Gottlieb sound board, which runs a second 6502 at 894 kHz plus Votrax SC-01 speech through its OWN bus_split! inside GottliebSoundBoard::tick. The main 8088 bus was never where Q*bert's time went. Filed as 61aj with the measurement.

Shapes: Atari System 1 kept the board and gave each game a view (Marble's trackball counters, Road Runner's joystick ADC), with the helpers that read them moving onto the views. Gottlieb's board became the bus outright, Q*bert being its only machine.

Both wide bus_split! arms are now unreferenced, and impl_board_delegation!'s bus_addr / 'bus_addr: u32 word' options are unused by any machine -- both get deleted with bus_split! itself in 642d. The design doc's prediction held again: nothing in either conversion was width-specific.

Also inverted the Atari System 1 frame loop (VBLANK IRQ4 + the motion-object scanline IRQ3 are the per-scanline work); Gottlieb needed no inversion, its only frame-position test being the end-of-frame render.

One test caught a real mistake in my rewrite: Road Runner's check_interrupts sets the IRQ2 line from the ADC before delegating to the board, so routing the test at the board directly reported irq_level 0. It goes through the view, like the CPU does.

Golden frames unchanged for all pinned machines; machine, harness and ROM-gated suites pass; clippy and fmt clean.

19 files still reference bus_split!, all in the 642d (standalone machines) bucket.

title: Williams machines never leave FACTORY SETTINGS RESTORED on a cold boot
description:
Captured while pinning golden frames (phosphor-emulator-frame-regression-w1pi.2). Booted from reset with no NVRAM, joust, robotron and sinistar print the CMOS-init message and stay on it: joust still shows 'FACTORY SETTINGS RESTORED' at 10000 frames (~166 emulated seconds). On hardware the message clears after a few seconds and the game drops into attract mode.

Loading a factory NVRAM works around it completely — with a dumped 1 KB CMOS image, joust reaches its title screen by frame 2400, robotron by 2400 and sinistar by 1800 — so the boards, blitter, palette and sound are fine. What is stuck is whatever the CMOS-init path waits on before continuing: a timer, an operator-switch read, or the post-init warm-start branch.

boot_check_test.rs does not catch it because the message itself is drawn pixels, which satisfies 'the machine drew something'.

Until it is fixed the three golden frames use committed NVRAM fixtures (harness/tests/golden/nvram/*.nv); once the cold boot reaches attract on its own, those entries can drop the fixture and be recaptured.

title: M6809: indexed indirect puts its don't-care cycles after the pointer read
description:
Found while doing phosphor-emulator-vy6l. Addresses are right, ORDER is not.

For an indirect indexed postbyte, the hardware forms the base address, spends
that mode's don't-care cycles, THEN reads the two pointer bytes, THEN spends one
final /VMA cycle:

    [base don't-cares]  ptr_hi  ptr_lo  $FFFF

`indexed_resolve` does it the other way round — states 10/11 read the pointer
first, and the whole don't-care countdown (state 20, plus the caller's base
don't-care) runs afterwards:

    ptr_hi  ptr_lo  [all don't-cares]

Cycle counts are identical, and every don't-care presents the address it should,
so nothing in cross-validation or the single-step vectors notices. What differs
is what an address-snooping device sees *between* the pointer read and the
don't-cares — and that ordering is exactly the kind of thing a slapstic decides
on. The chips on Atari System 1 (Marble Madness 103, Road Runner 108) are the
exposure; neither is verified against a reference here.

The fix is to split `indexed_resolve` so the base don't-cares are emitted before
the state-10 transition and exactly one /VMA remains after state 11. That also
lets the caller's base don't-care cycle (state 40 in every indexed op) fold back
into the resolver, which is where it belongs.

No known game depends on it, hence P3 — but it is a real difference from the
hardware, not a modelling choice.
close_reason: indexed_resolve now spends each mode's base don't-cares before the indirect pointer read, with exactly one trailing /VMA after it, and the caller's base don't-care (state 39/40 in every indexed op) folds back into the resolver. Cycle counts unchanged — rederived from the datasheet Table 2 '+' figures for all 24 modes, and confirmed by replaying the 266,000 single-step vectors: 10,549 traces reorder, none differ in registers, memory, cycle count, or read/write direction. Ordering pinned by 8 new cases in m6809_dont_care_cycle_test.rs. Commits a07ea73, 0804ee4.

title: Mario Bros: no sound — 8049 sound engine never enables timer/interrupts
description:
Mario Bros (mariobros) graphics, inputs, DMA, NVRAM all work, but there is no sound; the DAC path itself is dead (not just the deferred discrete circuit).

Findings (verified with the real mariog ROM):
- The 8049 sound CPU runs but is stuck in its sample-playback loop at PC 0x900-0x9FF, continuously writing DAC=0x00. Audio is a constant -32768 (3 distinct values over 2.2M samples).
- It NEVER enables timer/counter/TCNTI/interrupt across a full run (EVER all 0), though the sound ROM has STRT T / EN TCNTI / EN I at 0x062/0x070/0x379/0x04d.
- The main Z80 DOES request sounds (47 nonzero cmd writes to 0x7e00, 102 nonzero triggers to 0x7f00-0x7f07), so the Mario-side wiring is fine; the 8049 just never processes them (its timer-interrupt dispatch never starts).
- 8049 boot immediately CALLs ROM bank 1 (0x100) via SEL MB/DBF. Suspect a bug in the shared phosphor-core I8035 8049-mode execution: DBF/SEL-MBx (A11) addressing on CALL/JMP, interrupt vectoring (ext 0x003 / timer 0x007), or the P2/tune_r MOVX bank-select. I8035 changes need cross-validation.
- Still deferred regardless: discrete walk/skid analog sound (nl_mario.cpp) + the 0x7f07 skid trigger.

Repro: run mariobros, coin+start into gameplay; DAC stays 0x00.
close_reason: Fixed in cebacf6. Root cause: the M58715 sound CPU has an undumped internal-ROM bootstrap that runs before the external program; per MAME's audiocpu trace it does ANL P2,#$DF; SEL MB0; CALL $101, entering the external program at 0x101 (STRT T). We started at external 0x000, where the STRT T at 0x101 is swallowed as the JC operand at 0x100, so the sound engine's duration timer never started and every effect hung in its playback loop with a silent DAC. MarioBrosSystem::reset now replicates the bootstrap (P2=0xDF, MB0, PC=0x101). DAC output went from 3 distinct values to 20k+ across the full range — digitized SFX now play. Verified by diffing our 8049 PC trace against MAME -debugscript. Discrete walk/skid analog sound remains deferred (separate).

title: Dig Dug EAROM C1 control line decoded non-inverted, high scores never persist
close_reason: Fixed in machines/src/digdug.rs:957: C1 control line for the ER2055 EAROM is active-low on this hardware (MAME galaga.cpp: C1 = !BIT(data,1)), but was decoded non-inverted (data & 0x02 != 0). This swapped every EAROM mode — the game's WRITE commands became reads (score never stored) and READ commands ran destructive writes — so high scores never persisted. Changed to 'data & 0x02 == 0', matching MAME and the sibling astdelux machine (identical control-byte layout). title: Gottlieb sound board: the sound 6502 still dispatches through bus_split!
description:
GottliebSoundBoard::tick (machines/src/gottlieb.rs:~212) still runs its M6502 through 'bus_split!(self, bus => ...)' -- the sound board is a self-contained bus (RIOT + DAC + Votrax SC-01 + 8KB ROM) whose CPU sits inside it, exactly the shape the rollout has been removing one level up.

Why it matters, measured: converting Q*bert's *main* 8088 bus (926a5af) moved its frame time by 0.7%, against 12-15% for the Atari System 1 boards in the same commit. Q*bert's emulation time is ~2.8 ms/frame and almost all of it is the sound board -- a second 6502 at 894 kHz plus Votrax speech synthesis, all dispatching through this remaining trait object. This is where Q*bert's win actually is.

Shape: give GottliebBoard a 'sound_cpu: M6502' field (or a small SoundCpu wrapper), have GottliebSoundBoard keep only the devices, and pass the CPU into tick -- 'sound.tick(&mut sound_cpu)'. The board is the bus; no view needed, since nothing is interposed. Follow docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md.

Watch: the sound board is saved as part of GottliebBoard's state, so moving the CPU field changes save layout unless the CPU is written in the same position (it is currently written by GottliebSoundBoard::save_state -- check the order before/after).

Measure qbert with phosphor-bench before and after; golden frames should be unchanged, but the Votrax/RIOT NMI edge timing is worth a careful look since the sound CPU's cycle boundaries are what drive it.

title: Concrete bus dispatch: Williams (Joust, Robotron, Sinistar)
description:
Convert the Williams 2nd-gen board (M6809 + M6800 sound + blitter) per docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md. Blocked by the generic Cpu::reset task (the M6809 fetches its reset vector through the bus).

This is the second-bus-master case: the blitter drives the bus as BusMaster::Dma/DmaVram from inside the board, so it re-enters through &mut self and needs no split -- but DmaVram deliberately bypasses banking, so keep the two masters distinguishable through any read-path refactor. Measure joust before/after; run golden frames.
notes: Also do the scanline-outer / cycle-inner inversion here. williams.rs:465 was the third site listed in concrete-bus-dispatch-blzz.5; the Namco boards were inverted in 2b1667f and Williams was left out because it still dispatches through bus_split!, so the two changes belong together. On the Namco boards the inversion was worth a further 7-18% on top of the dispatch change.
close_reason:
Done in 9d19a4f (joust + robotron + sinistar together -- they share WilliamsBoard).

Numbers (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, best of 6 alternating runs, idle host):
  joust    0.634 -> 0.612 ms/f  -3.5%
  robotron 0.636 -> 0.593       -6.8%
  sinistar 0.778 -> 0.735       -5.5%
Smaller than the Namco boards' 12-27%, and expected: at 1 MHz these run a third as many cycles per frame, so more of the frame is the scanline renderer and the per-cycle audio path (DAC + CVSD + resampler), which neither change touches.

Shape: CPUs move out of the board onto each machine as separate fields (so the debug derive sees one #[debug_cpu] each, and the save-state layout is unchanged -- the board wrote its CPUs first, so no SAVE_VERSION bump). WilliamsCpus is a borrowed pair passed to a generic williams::tick. Robotron and Sinistar add nothing to the board's decoding, so WilliamsBoard implements Bus and IS their bus (no view). Joust needs a view for its LS157 mux; its per-cycle mux update became the WilliamsBus::begin_cycle hook, so the debugger's single-step gets it too.

The second-bus-master answer: the blitter lives *inside* the bus it drives, so it is lifted out of the board with mem::replace for its DMA cycle and put back after -- the safe equivalent of the aliasing this used to rely on. Nothing else observes the gap (only that cycle runs; the halt line it feeds is read by the main CPU, which is not stepping). One behavior difference: a blit whose destination walked into 0xCA00-0xCA07 would lose the write, where the aliased version corrupted the live blitter. No game does that; a debug_assert in bus_write catches it if one ever does. DmaVram still bypasses banking as before.

First real user of the generic Cpu::reset (bek7): the M6809 fetches its reset vector through the bus, so both CPUs now reset against the machine's own bus.

Also did the scanline-outer / cycle-inner inversion left here by blzz.5: rendering a line and driving the ROM PIA video timing signals now happen 260x per frame instead of on each of 16,640 cycles.

New public surface on the three machines: bus_read/bus_write (CPU-facing, side effects included -- distinct from BusDebug peek/poke) and get_cpu_state/get_sound_cpu_state, replacing what tests reached through the system's Bus impl and the board's CPU fields. Worth reusing as the convention for the remaining conversions. The board's device-index tests moved up to the machine, where they now cover the CPU/board join in the derive.

Golden frames unchanged for all 39 machines (these three are blitter-drawn), plus machine, harness and ROM-gated suites; clippy and fmt clean.

title: Q*Bert MOB colors wrong: sprite bitplanes flipped vs MAME (LSB/MSB plane order)
description:
Q*Bert's motion-object (sprite/MOB) colors are wrong — the 4 sprite bitplanes
are flipped relative to MAME, permuting the 16 colors of every sprite by a
bit-reversal of the pen index. Same bug class as the Food Fight fix (commit
7978ad5): phosphor's decode_gfx orders plane_offsets LSB-first (entry 0 = pen
bit 0), the reverse of MAME's MSB-first planeoffset, so a machine that copies
MAME's plane list verbatim ends up with reversed planes.

Root cause — machines/src/gottlieb.rs, GottliebBoard::decode_gfx (~line 510):
    let planes: [usize; 4] = std::array::from_fn(|p| p * quarter * 8);
    // plane_offsets = [0, q*8, 2q*8, 3q*8]  (LSB-first: bit0 <- ROM quarter 0)

MAME (src/mame/gottlieb/gottlieb.cpp:2130 spr_layout):
    { RGN_FRAC(0,4), RGN_FRAC(1,4), RGN_FRAC(2,4), RGN_FRAC(3,4) }
    // MSB-first: planeoffset[0] = pen bit 3 <- ROM quarter 0

MAME maps bit3<-Q0, bit2<-Q1, bit1<-Q2, bit0<-Q3; phosphor maps bit0<-Q0 ...
bit3<-Q3 — every pen index p becomes bitrev4(p) (0<->0,1<->8,2<->4,3<->12,...),
scrambling each sprite's 16-color set.

Isolated to sprites: the tile layout in the same file (GOTTLIEB_TILE_LAYOUT,
plane_offsets [3,2,1,0]) IS correctly reversed vs MAME's gfx_8x8x4_packed_msb
(planeoffset {0,1,2,3} = STEP4(0,1), src/emu/video/generic.cpp:97), so tiles
render correctly. Sprite x_offsets/y_offsets/char_increment all match MAME
(STEP16(0,1)/STEP16(0,16)/32*8) — plane order is the only difference.

Scope: GottliebBoard::decode_gfx is used only by Q*Bert (machines/src/qbert.rs).
acceptance_criteria:
* Q*Bert MOBs (Q*Bert, Coily, balls, Slick/Sam, discs) render with MAME-matching
  colors; compare a screenshot to a MAME reference frame.
* Tile/playfield colors unchanged (already correct).
* cargo test -p phosphor-machines, clippy, and fmt pass.
close_reason: Fixed in 3ad18aa: reversed Q*Bert sprite plane order in GottliebBoard::decode_gfx to [3q,2q,q,0]*8 (LSB-first, matching MAME spr_layout's MSB-first planeoffset). Verified by user.

title: Asteroids sound fidelity: thrust rumble + MAME output post-processing
description:
Follow-up polish from the Asteroids discrete-sound migration (l7o.3). See docs/debugging-asteroids-discrete-sound.md and tools/sound-reference/.

SYMPTOM
- By ear, thrust does not rumble enough, even though its band centre (~85 Hz) matches MAME's measured ~82 Hz peak / 128 Hz centroid. So it's not a pitch error — it's missing low-end weight/body.

HYPOTHESIS: MAME output post-processing
- MAME 0.287's new audio system applies a per-game <audio_effects> chain AFTER the discrete mix. ~/mame/cfg/asteroid.cfg shows: Filters, Compressor, Reverb, Equalizer on tag ':mono'. A compressor + low-shelf EQ would lift and thicken the sub-bass rumble in the *played* sound vs the raw netlist output.
- Open question: does '-wavwrite' tap the speaker mix BEFORE or AFTER that effects chain? If after, our captured 'ground truth' already includes the effects and Phosphor should match the post-effect sound. If before, the difference vs what the user hears is the effects chain.

INVESTIGATION
1. Capture MAME thrust with the audio_effects chain enabled vs disabled (clear/zero the effects in cfg, or a fresh cfg) and compare spectra — quantify how much low-end the compressor/EQ adds.
2. Determine the wavwrite tap point (pre/post effects) from MAME 0.287 source or by toggling effects and diffing captures.
3. Decide whether Phosphor should model an output-stage low-shelf/compressor (in the discrete framework's output stage, reusable across boards) to match the played sound, vs. matching only the raw netlist.

SECONDARY (from the case-study open threads)
- Consider wiring the Phosphor-vs-MAME centroid comparison (tools/sound-reference + machines/examples/asteroid_capture.rs) as a checked-in tolerance test, gated/local-only since it needs MAME + ROMs.

NON-GOAL: bit-exact audio. Target is matching the audible character (the deep thrust rumble) within tolerance.

Board now logs (scanline,mo_bank) transitions per frame and render_motion_objects renders each scanline band with the bank live there (clipping sprites to the band), mirroring MAME's partial-render-then-switch; Marble byte-identical (single-bank). 2 board unit tests + user-verified in-game. title: Epic: Rebuild the audio output path
description:
The chips are modelled far better than they are heard. POKEY steps four LFSRs at 1.79 MHz, and the Namco WSG, AY-8910, SN76489 and TMS5220 are comparably faithful — then every one of them hands output to AudioResampler, which decimates to 44.1 kHz by averaging a box of samples (roughly 40 wide for POKEY, 70 for a 3.07 MHz Namco board).

A box filter is a poor anti-aliasing filter: first sidelobe about 13 dB down, no real stopband. Square-wave harmonic energy above 22 kHz folds back into the audible band as inharmonic content. This is the single largest gap between how carefully the hardware is modelled and how it sounds.

Four smaller defects sit in the same path and are cheapest to fix together: no audio/video clock synchronisation, a mutex taken on the real-time audio thread, a hardcoded 44_100 output rate, and an O(n) memmove per drain.

Design: docs/designs/audio-output-path.md

Contained to core/src/audio/ and frontend/src/audio.rs plus per-device constructor signatures. No machine logic changes. Best audible improvement per line in the review.

title: Replace box-filter decimation with two-stage polyphase FIR
description:
core/src/audio/mod.rs:124 — AudioResampler::tick box-averages input samples and emits the mean. See the epic and design doc for why that aliases.

Fix (design doc section 3): two-stage decimation. Keep the cheap box down to roughly 4x the target rate, then a windowed-sinc / polyphase FIR to the output rate. Cost is a few dozen multiply-adds per OUTPUT sample, not per input cycle, so the per-emulated-cycle hot path is unchanged.

Keep the existing API (tick, tick_sample, push_sample, fill_audio, drain_audio, set_input_rate) so no device or board changes.

Preserve the upsampling path: core/src/audio/mod.rs:253 pins the TMS5220 case (8,135 Hz in, 44.1 kHz out) that a downsample-only resampler broke before.

Acceptance: a test asserting stopband rejection — feed a tone above the output Nyquist, assert the aliased energy in the output is at least 60 dB down. Also compare a recorded WAV of a known machine before/after by ear.

title: Negotiate the real output sample rate instead of hardcoding 44_100
description:
Every sound device constructs its resampler against a literal or per-file const 44_100:
  core/src/device/ay8910.rs:106, namco_wsg.rs:64, konami_sound.rs:64, ssio.rs:49,
  tms5220.rs:46, votrax_sc01.rs:59, machines/src/congo_bongo.rs:98
and frontend/src/audio.rs:94 asks SDL for that rate but discards the spec it is actually granted.

On a device that opens at 48 kHz the whole machine plays about 8 percent sharp and drains its ring 8 percent too fast.

POKEY already has the right shape — Pokey::with_clock(clock_hz, sample_rate) — so this is generalising an existing pattern, not inventing one.

Fix: thread the granted spec.freq back through AudioSource::audio_sample_rate() and into device construction. AudioResampler::set_input_rate shows the retune pattern for the other direction.

Acceptance: forcing SDL to 48 kHz produces correct pitch.

title: Lock-free SPSC ring between the emulator and the SDL audio callback
description:
frontend/src/audio.rs:26 — the SDL audio callback runs on a real-time thread and locks a Mutex<VecDeque<i16>> shared with the emulator thread. If the emulator holds that lock when the callback fires, the audio thread blocks and the buffer underruns: priority inversion, the classic cause of intermittent crackle that never reproduces under a debugger.

The drain-then-release structure narrows the window but cannot remove it.

Fix: a lock-free SPSC ring — two atomics over a fixed [i16; N]. Roughly 60 lines, no new dependency, removes the failure mode rather than shrinking it.

Acceptance: no lock, allocation or syscall on the callback path. Keep the existing fade-in/fade-out and hold-last-sample-on-underrun behaviour.

title: Close the audio/video clock loop with ring-fill feedback
description:
Video is paced off the host monotonic clock against frame_rate_hz (frontend/src/emulator.rs:1203); audio is consumed off the sound card crystal. Those clocks differ by tens of ppm on real hardware and nothing reconciles them.

When the producer runs ahead the ring drops its oldest samples (emulator.rs:916, buf.pop_front()); when it runs behind the callback holds the last sample (audio.rs:41). Both are audible, and both recur on a period set by drift rate rather than by anything in the game.

Fix (design doc section 5): feed ring fill level back into the resampler output rate as a small trim, roughly +/-0.5 percent, so the producer tracks the consumer. AudioResampler::set_input_rate already supports runtime retuning.

Depends on the SPSC ring sibling (fill level must be readable without a lock) and the rate-negotiation sibling.

Acceptance: run a machine for 30 minutes and assert zero dropped-sample events and zero underruns.

title: Resampler output should be a ring, not a Vec drained with drain(..n)
description:
core/src/audio/mod.rs:192 — fill_audio drains with Vec::drain(..n), shifting every remaining element down on each call. Small in absolute terms at one call per frame, but it is a ring buffer wearing a Vec costume, and multi-chip boards pay it once per device (Star Wars and I Robot have four POKEYs each).

Fix: VecDeque or a plain ring. Lands naturally alongside the polyphase rework, which touches the same struct.

Acceptance: no per-call memmove of the backlog; existing resampler tests still pass unchanged.

title: Add Battlezone (Atari b/w vector, M6502 + DVG + Mathbox)
description: Atari Battlezone (1980) arcade machine. Hardware: M6502 + DVG b/w vector generator + Mathbox coprocessor + POKEY. All devices (M6502, DVG, Mathbox, POKEY) are already implemented and validated, so this is largely board wiring + ROM definitions. First shipping machine to exercise the Mathbox. See README Future > Games.

title: Make Cpu::reset generic over the bus type
description:
Cpu::reset takes '&mut Self::Bus' where BusMasterComponent::Bus is the associated type 'dyn Bus<Address = .., Data = ..>', implicitly 'static. A borrowed bus view (the concrete-dispatch shape) cannot be passed to it -- its lifetime cannot be named -- so every board whose CPU fetches a reset vector through the bus is blocked: M6502, M6809, M68000 (M6502 reads 0xFFFC/0xFFFD, M6809 reads 0xFFFE/0xFFFF).

Both prototypes sidestepped it because the Z80 ignores the bus at reset: Pac-Man resets against the board, Galaga uses Z80::hardware_reset.

Shape:
  fn reset<B: Bus<Address = Self::Address, Data = Self::Data> + ?Sized>(&mut self, bus: &mut B, master: BusMaster)
which needs Address/Data associated types on Cpu (or a similar bound). Makes Cpu non-object-safe -- no dyn Cpu exists in the workspace, so that costs nothing.

Touches every CPU impl and every reset call site. First task of the rollout; blocks steps 5-9 in docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md.
close_reason:
Done in 5bbae94.

Instead of keeping 'type Bus = dyn Bus<..>' and bounding reset by <Self::Bus as Bus>::Address, the associated type is now the bus *widths*: BusMasterComponent carries 'type Address' and 'type Data', and both tick_with_bus and Cpu::reset take 'B: Bus<Address = Self::Address, Data = Self::Data> + ?Sized'. That removes the trait object from the trait entirely rather than working around it, and makes tick_with_bus monomorphise too.

?Sized keeps '&mut dyn Bus' a legal argument, so every board still on bus_split! compiles untouched and the rollout can proceed one board at a time. Both traits lose object safety; nothing used dyn Cpu or dyn BusMasterComponent (verified by grep across the workspace).

Call-site churn was small: the seven CPU impls, the Cpu trait, and simple_system.rs's generic bounds (BusMasterComponent<Bus = dyn Bus<..>> -> BusMasterComponent<Address = u16, Data = u8>).

Payoff demonstrated immediately: Ms. Pac-Man dropped its workaround and now resets through its own borrowed bus view.

New regression test core/tests/cpu_bus_generic_test.rs: a 6502 and a 6809 reset through a borrowed view (reading their reset vectors), a cycle runs against one, and a &mut dyn Bus is still accepted. If the signatures ever go back to an associated dyn type, that file stops compiling.

Verification: phosphor-core, phosphor-machines, phosphor-macros, phosphor-frontend, phosphor-cpu-validation (including the slow single-step validators) and the ROM-gated harness suites all pass; golden frames unchanged for all 39 machines; clippy and fmt clean. The C++ cross-validator matches its documented baseline (M6809 99.28%, known indexed-mode cycle-table FIXME) -- unaffected, since this is a signature-only refactor and the committed vectors are unchanged. (The m6800/i8035 validator binaries in cross-validation/bin are stale builds for another platform and will not exec; that predates this change.)

Unblocks 8v1a (Williams), hv5p (Atari DVG/AVG), 3hnp (Atari System 1 + Gottlieb), 642d (standalone + delete bus_split!).
